script:
The sky above Rwanda's rolling hills carries more than clouds—it carries hope. Every three minutes, a drone launches from a distribution center, racing life-saving blood and medical supplies to remote hospitals unreachable by road. This is Africa's drone revolution in action.

While the world debates drone regulations, Rwanda became the first country to operate a national drone delivery network. Zipline's autonomous aircraft have completed over 400,000 flights, delivering blood in thirteen minutes instead of four hours by road. Nigeria and Ghana quickly followed, transforming healthcare delivery across impossible terrains.

But Africa isn't just importing solutions—it's creating them. South African startup Aerobotics uses AI-powered drones to scan millions of acres of farmland, helping farmers detect pests and diseases before they spread. In Morocco, ATLAN Space manufactures surveillance drones entirely on African soil. Kenya's Astral Aerial has mapped refugee camps and tracked wildlife poachers from above.

This skyward revolution has created over 5,000 direct jobs and trained a new generation of African drone pilots and engineers. From Malawi testing mosquito net deliveries to Tanzania surveying crops with locally-built drones, Africa has leapfrogged traditional infrastructure constraints.

The continent that skipped landlines for mobile phones is now bypassing roads for airways. In Africa's skies, drones aren't just gadgets—they're lifelines, connecting the unconnected and proving that sometimes, the best way forward is up.
